style: former prop trader (Datek) and multi-strategy hedge fund manager
edge_principles: Bubble-era momentum traders who could not adapt once the regime turned gave back most gains; a style tied to one regime needs a regime check.
In prop, a commission markup on trader volume acted as a loss buffer for the firm; costs paid per trade are a real drag that must be modeled.
Trading on 'smart money is buying' tips carries legal and reputational tail risk; base trades on own, documented signals.
notes: Story of an insider-trading arrest, trial and prison time. No trading setups discussed.

style: prop trader, cross-border ADR arbitrage, delta-neutral pairs, options spreads on catalysts
markets: Japanese stocks and their US ADRs, US options
edge_principles: Prop capital does not allow slow losses the way a hedge fund does; cut losers fast and prefer delta-neutral structures when learning.
Dislocation strategies need volatility; on quiet days algos price things correctly, so trade less and wait for earnings or vol events.
Less-crowded, less-liquid listings (OTC, five-letter ADRs) hold more dislocations because algos avoid them.
Gap risk at the next open (limit moves) can make one trade cost months of profit; size for the open gap, not the intraday range.
Defined-risk structures (option spreads) let you know the max loss at entry.
Check a prop firm's fee load; per-share fees can turn a profitable month into a small payout.
notes: Explains ADR/home-market arbitrage around earnings; mostly not testable with MCF data. Beta-pair idea on crash days is the only partly testable piece.

style: host conference talk summarising prior guests
edge_principles: Only trade where you have an edge: a trade repeated hundreds of times should end with more money.
Even with a clear edge, over-betting causes ruin (biased-coin experiment: about a third of smart participants went bust betting a 60/40 coin); size bets well below full Kelly.
Returns are concentrated: 5-20% of trades often make most of the year's profit, so risk control on the rest keeps you alive for the outliers; do not cap winners.
Specialise; know why the strategy makes money so you can hold through drawdowns; 'do less, do it better, do it bigger'.
Know your exit before entry; judge yourself on following process, not on single-trade outcome.
A turtle trader said he would be richer had he always followed his systems; deviation from tested rules costs money.
Filter every change by 'does this raise profitability or cut risk?'
notes: Host's talk distilling six habits of successful guests. No setups.

guest: Ryan Moffett, Tyler Micalove, Wayne Klump
style: small options fund (Black Pier Capital), index option structures, volatility-based
edge_principles: Before adding a strategy, demand 50 to ~1000 backtest data points plus drawdown, scalability and liquidity estimates.
Map each strategy to five market scenarios (down hard, down slow, flat, up slow, up hard) and combine strategies whose good scenarios differ.
High-probability premium selling (e.g. put credit spreads) makes small steady gains then gives back months in one move; judge payoff asymmetry, not win rate.
A directional strategy with only ~54% accuracy can be the top earner if trade management makes winners much larger than losers.
Execution errors are costly at size: use a two-person pilot/co-pilot check and checklists before orders go out.
Emotion fell sharply when traders executed each other's accounts; hide live P&L and follow the rules mechanically.
Define the goal (return, drawdown, regime) first; it rules out strategy families that can never meet it.
Keep a permanent, low-drag tail hedge rather than repeatedly buying outright puts.
notes: Team/mentoring discussion and options-portfolio construction; no concrete testable intraday setups.

style: quant developer/trader (prop, funds), factor models, trend following
edge_principles: Overfitting check (system parameter permutation): run EVERY parameter set through both train and test periods and regress test P&L/Sharpe on train P&L/Sharpe; a real signal shows correlation across the whole grid, including bad sets staying bad; a round blob means no information.

Build-rebuild-compare: backtest many random one-year windows inside the full history; the gap between the window-average and the full-period result estimates live shortfall and sets a 'switch-off' drawdown threshold.
Sample parameter space randomly (Monte Carlo) instead of a nested grid so an early stop still covers the space evenly.
Rank factors by Spearman information coefficient vs forward returns; information ratio ~ IC x sqrt(breadth), so more names/trades raises IR for the same IC.
Short-horizon retail trading is hard after spreads and commissions; pure price-action edges are decaying, so longer-horizon or alternative-data factors are attractive.
ML alone rarely runs a full strategy; use ML outputs as one factor among several with economic rationale.
notes: Strategy-development and robustness methods (directly relevant to MCF research rules), plus AI/quantum computing talk. No concrete setups.

style: independent discretionary order-flow scalper
edge_principles: Most losing days come from forcing trades during slow periods when nothing matches the plan; doing nothing is part of the job.
Know where the trade is wrong before entry; never widen a stop, since a 3-tick loss turns into an 8-tick loss.
Exit on evidence that the move has stalled instead of letting a trailing stop give back profits.
All-in/all-out sizing avoids the trap of scaling out of winners and averaging into losers, which inverts risk/reward.
Adjust approach by day context: payroll/news days vs quiet Mondays need different expectations and trade counts.
Specialise in one market to learn the habits of its main players.
Use stop-market (not stop-limit) emergency stops so a fast move cannot skip your exit.
Shorter holds are easier to predict than multi-hour holds; HFT chain reactions through stop clusters can reshape the day.
Replaying recorded sessions around turning points teaches faster than a trade journal.
notes: Explains order-book reading for Treasury futures. Setups need Level 2 / tick data, so they are not testable in MCF.

style: risk manager (AQR), former poker player, options floor trader, PM
edge_principles: Formal drawdown-control policy: pre-commit to cut risk by a set fraction (e.g. 20%) at set loss levels and re-add once price recovers a little from its low; long-run P&L is about the same but the low points are shallower and decisions are not forced.
Never size so large that losses force you to cut; a small early risk cut (5%) can let you stay in a good trade through a crisis.
Backtests run over a period when money is flowing into a strategy overstate return and understate risk; crowded factors all lose together when money leaves (Aug 2007 quant crash).
Prefer idiosyncratic signals that others do not use; widely known factors were hit hardest in the 2007 unwind.
Risk management is about using risk well (when to swing big vs play small), not only minimising it.
Seek markets that are new or less competitive, where a clear mathematical edge exists, rather than competing with veterans.
notes: Part 1 of Aaron Brown's risk-management interview: background, role of risk managers, 2007 quant equity crisis. No setups.

style: risk manager (AQR), quant
edge_principles: Pick the payoff ratio (avg win / avg loss) and stick to it; let the market set the win rate. Shrinking targets or widening stops to restore a falling win rate is usually disastrous.
Before any trade, name both numbers: how much it makes if right and how far it must move against you to prove you wrong.
Spend more planning effort on exits for winners (fast vs slow moves) than on capping losers; most money is left on the table on the upside.
Once a strategy is approved, pick a size and keep it; starting tiny and scaling up after it 'proves itself' leaves you largest exactly when the edge fades.
Risk limits should only bind when survival is at stake; limits that trigger on ordinary bad days kill more opportunity than risk.
Judge risks by the median outcome under average luck, not the mean; beyond the Kelly point more risk only adds bad outcomes.
Size with Kelly using max loss if wrong and estimated edge; track realised edge and realised loss vs plan and resize from them.
High-win-rate premium-collecting strategies must reserve profits for the rare big loss; low-win-rate strategies must be sure someone can pay the big win.
Keep 3-5 stress scenarios (cash freeze, no trading access, counterparty failure, bad prices) with contingency plans, rather than trying to predict black swans.
notes: Part 2 of Aaron Brown: practical risk thinking (payoff ratio, Kelly, VaR, black swans). No setups.

style: trading-technology CEO (Trading Technologies), not a trader
edge_principles: Any automated strategy needs pre-deployment checks: test against known history for runaway order loops, risk-limit breaches and over-messaging before it goes live.
Hard, granular risk controls outside the strategy logic contain the damage when the logic is wrong.
Code written in a hurry for live use is risky; separate the request from the deployment and test first.
If you cannot be the fastest, compete by being first to an idea, safer, or by using your own trade data to trade smarter.
notes: Trading technology, latency race, ML-based trade surveillance, MiFID II algo testing. No setups.

style: retail part-time systematic trader
edge_principles: Match the rule family (momentum vs mean reversion) to the asset and bar interval; the same RSI rule flips sign depending on regime.
Keep strategies simple: 2-6 inputs, under ~50 lines of code, to stay robust.
Mean-reversion systems often do better without hard stops and fixed targets; use indicator exits.
Overriding the system after a surprise event (2016 election) missed a 30-40% run; do not switch off a tested system on opinion.
Automated systems still need daily health checks (API/broker disconnects caused an unnoticed drawdown).
Start live with a small fraction of capital for walk-forward confidence before scaling.
notes: Simple RSI-based ETF systems selected by a momentum/mean-reversion regime scan; partly testable in MCF on ETFs. Reported returns rely on inverse-vol ETNs (which later blew up in Feb 2018).

style: quant research analyst (commodity futures fund), academic asset pricing
edge_principles: Screen ideas fast: design the sharpest test that could reject the idea and spend at most 1-2 days; this discards 70-80% of ideas.
Start with summary stats, plots and a simple linear regression; a robust effect should show up without fancy models.
Expect live decay vs backtest; measure it (e.g. backtest Sharpe 2.5 -> live 1.0 = 60% decay = untrustworthy; 1.5 -> 1.2 = robust).
Judge strategies on return, vol, Sharpe, max drawdown and tail correlation (what it did in crashes like late 2008).
Trading costs, turnover, market impact and rebalance timing can matter as much as the premium itself; academic factor results ignore them.
Rebalance when liquidity is deep (e.g. alongside index rebalances) to cut costs.
Read papers for the 'big question' and keep an idea notebook; but actually test ideas rather than only reading.
notes: Research-process episode; one position-horizon SPY timing idea. Strong alignment with MCF research rules (costs in, out-of-sample decay).

style: ex-bank derivatives/relative-value trader; ML-driven sports-betting fund
edge_principles: Look for markets with fragmented liquidity, retail-dominated flow and little professional capital; edges are larger there.
A small, consistent edge is enough: realising ~52-53% where the market prices 50% is profitable over a season of many bets.
Scalability trades off against edge: smaller venues are less efficient but cap position size.
Trade late, when information is complete and liquidity deepest; professionals let the public move prices first.
Watch whether price moves are proportionate to traded volume to infer informed flow.
Arbitrage gaps are better used as a signal (which side the book wants to offload) than as the trade itself when margins are tiny.
Remove emotional attachment; treat each event as a security.
notes: Applying trading principles and ML to sports betting. No stock/ETF setups.

style: former CBOE options floor trader, serial entrepreneur and investor
edge_principles: Someone must clearly own monitoring of each trader/position; a trader doubled down while two partners each assumed the other was watching and lost millions.
Keep passive positions small enough that the worst case does not demand attention.
Break a large book into low-risk, defined-risk pieces and focus attention on the pieces that carry risk.
Prefer limited-downside, open-upside structures (option-like thinking) in any investment.
Most active traders fail (~90%); mentored traders with tested strategies, money management and tools succeed far more often.
notes: Business and wealth-building discussion. No trading setups.

style: prop day trader/partner (Seven Points Capital); momentum and scalping
markets: US stocks (large caps, low-price high-volume, low-cap runners), some futures/options
edge_principles: Each setup gets written rules for scan, entry, scaling, stop and size; grade each day on rule-following, not only P&L.
Take every valid instance of a setup; skipping some adds variance and frustration.
Throttle risk: cut to a quarter or half size when breaking rules or not reading the market well; size up to multiples only when in sync.
Know the exit before entry; place the stop where the pattern is invalidated and size from a fixed dollar risk.
Best trades work right away; decide whether a trade becomes a swing by whether it is green and acting right by the close.
Volume at price (volume profile) adds weight to support/resistance levels.
Journal and screenshot every occurrence of a setup; confidence and early recognition come from repetition.
Profits shifted from rebate/scalp edges (taken over by HFT) to momentum and catalyst trading.
notes: Practical prop day-trading episode with three setups; pullback-to-support and triangle breakdown are partly testable on 5-min bars.

style: retail full-time intraday breakout trader, long-biased
edge_principles: Scan for relative volume (>= 2.5x average); a perfect chart nobody is watching does not move.
Rank the watchlist A/B/C; trade C setups only when the market is risk-on, otherwise wait for A setups.
Days with no or few trades are fine; forcing trades on slow days used to erase a week's gains.
Take a partial right into the breakout and be ready to exit the rest at break-even; breakouts often fail.
If an order error puts you in a position you did not intend, exit at market immediately; fighting it caused most big losses.
Larger size needs a liquidity plan: low-float stocks may have no bid when you need to exit.
Be a small, separate allocation on the less-familiar side (shorts at ~1/20 size, one entry, fixed stop).
Crowding signal: when non-traders ask about the theme, reduce risk and shorten holding times.
notes: Simple, testable breakout process on high-rvol small caps; very strong results came in a speculative 2017 mania, so regime dependence is likely.

style: independent full-time small-cap short seller
edge_principles: Review annual results trade by trade: removing big avoidable losses (non-top setups at full size, letting losses grow) raised returns 50-75% without more risk.
Concentrate size in the few A+ setups that make most of the year; trade everything else small.
Increase size on top setups gradually (10-15% steps), not in one jump.
Never add to a losing short; add only when the trade is in your favour.
Take small 'paper cut' losses on early entries and re-enter later; the timing of tops is hard.
Front side of a squeeze is for small size; wait for the backside to size up.
Short sellers should spread across several brokers for locates and lower borrow fees; borrow costs can eat 10-15%+ of profits.
Drawing profits out regularly into illiquid, low-maintenance assets protects against a career-ending blow-up.
Small-cap runners dry up during earnings season; take more time off then.
notes: Parabolic-runner short strategy on low floats; partly testable if MCF has low-cap coverage and borrow cost assumptions.

style: oil derivatives market maker and discretionary prop trader (Onyx Commodities)
markets: Brent/WTI futures, dated Brent and product swaps
edge_principles: Use a structured improvement loop (Toyota Kata / plan-do-check-act): name specific obstacles, hypothesise a fix, run small experiments, review weekly.
Turn a 'view' into a hypothesis that includes positioning and regime (trending vs volatile, macro- vs fundamentals-driven).
Avoid the crowded side; when nearly everyone is positioned one way, reversals are violent and fading the crowd can work.
Place the stop where the hypothesis is proven wrong, outside normal volatility for the expected holding time, then size so that stop equals the allowed risk.
Cap total risk (e.g. 10% of capital) and per-trade risk (a fraction of that); expect to be wrong often.
Never average into a losing position; buy strength, sell weakness rather than anchoring on 'too high/too low'.
Know exactly what the contract prices off (e.g. Brent settles on a handful of North Sea fields); local events can dominate.
The regime of what drives price (macro vs physical) changes; re-check which drivers matter now.
Market-making flow is an information edge: seeing who needs to hedge reveals direction.
notes: Oil swaps/futures market structure and trader development. No stock setups.

style: venture capital (DRW VC), not a trader
edge_principles: Track runway and burn to see problems early so there are no surprises; plan funding before cash is under 12 months.
Value comes from forward cash flows; past traction informs projections, and management quality can veto a cheap price.
Most ICO-style opportunities were low quality with long lockups; perceived liquidity often did not exist.
notes: Venture capital at a trading firm; no trading content.

style: fixed-income relative value / global macro, discretionary with systematic execution
markets: Treasury futures and cash, index futures, crypto
edge_principles: Define risk from the planned entry before trading; if the stop needed at that entry is too large, cut size or wait for a better level.
Reduce size and activity in erratic, headline-driven regimes or when you cannot afford a drawdown.
Short-volatility products and option-selling strategies work for years and then blow up; hard risk limits must exist outside the strategy.
Percentage moves in VIX are much larger when it starts very low; liquidation thresholds keyed to % moves get hit more easily.
Most time goes into research, only a small share into trading; trade only when technical levels agree with the fundamental view.
Allow three choices on every idea: buy, sell or do nothing.
notes: Macro/relative-value discussion and 2018 short-vol blow-up; two loosely specified setups.

style: prop firm co-founder (SMB Capital), active equities
edge_principles: Develop in stages: consistency first, then size, then breadth (same edge in more names), then sophistication (e.g. options); most traders try to size before they are consistent.
Tag every trade by setup, measure results per setup, then trade the profitable setups more and drop the rest; capital increases should be justified by per-setup equity curves.

Keep a playbook: each archived setup records big-picture market context, daily technicals, intraday position vs opening range, catalyst, tape, plan and intuition; aim for 80%+ of trades from the playbook.
Daily report card on one monthly goal (e.g. a cap on losses on the 'front side' of a fading short) with concrete fixes; share it for accountability.
Cap risk on the front side of a counter-trend trade and put the bigger risk on the backside, once momentum confirms.
Scale risk up in roughly 20% steps after success, keeping the same per-trade percentages; jumping 1k to 5k daily risk tends to end in a crash.
When volatility regimes change (low-vol to high-vol), shift to the products that now move (SPY, QQQ, VXX) and accept they trade less cleanly.
Use technology: scanners/alerts for your best setups, scripted entries with discretionary exits, and backtests of the alert itself with simple exit rules.
Substantial P&L usually takes until about year three even with good support.
notes: Trader development framework from SMB Capital; no single concrete setup but strongly relevant process ideas (per-setup tagging, playbook, alerts->backtests).

style: veteran ex-floor scalper and interest-rate spread trader
markets: Australian interest-rate futures (bank bills, 3-yr/10-yr bonds), US grains historically
edge_principles: Scale size step by step; the first time at a larger size usually loses, so step back and retry later.
Process a loss, learn from it and let it go; dwelling on the last trade harms the next one.
Never lose all your capital; staying in the game is the first rule.
Cross-market divergences can warn early (e.g. Aug 2007 bank bills vs bonds blew out, 13 months before the 2008 crash).
When a relationship you trade breaks its normal band and you do not understand why, stop trading it.
Strategies must change as markets change; passive market-making edges disappeared once algos took queue priority.
Cut commissions as far as possible; they are a major trading cost.
Watch for a self-sabotage pattern after long winning runs (nine good months lost in three days).
Grow trading size only as market liquidity allows.
notes: Live event with a veteran spread trader; mostly mindset. One spread-divergence idea portable to ETF pairs.

style: independent ASX day trader, catalyst scalper, short-biased
edge_principles: Start with one setup you can do well (his was jumping the opening-auction surplus bid for a free look), grow size on it, and use the time it buys to learn others; that edge later faded.
Size by tick value and by liquidity in the book; avoid positions larger than the resting size that would protect your exit.
Cut immediately when a trade goes red; re-enter later if still valid; this kept losses small.
Don't fade on the front side before evidence of a turn; enter when flow shifts.
Most profit comes in the first 30-60 minutes; trade smaller later in the day.
Avoid trading against the obvious direction of a strong positive catalyst (short bias was a weakness).
Identify A+ setups in real time and hold them longer; covering early to lock P&L left most of the move.
Paper trading hides deficiencies; trade tiny real size to learn execution and loss handling.
Mentorship shortened the learning curve dramatically.
notes: Fast-ramping ASX scalper; catalyst-short and gap read-through ideas map to MCF as proxies without a news feed.

style: event-driven equity trader (M&A, activism, earnings, research flow)
markets: US stocks above $500M market cap, some options
edge_principles: Trade only stocks with a fresh reason for their value to change today (earnings, rulings, approvals, deals, influential research); random daily moves are unpredictable.
Avoid sub-$500M market caps: thin, easily manipulated, irrational participants.
Do not fade news (short good news / buy bad news because 'it moved too much'); big funds keep selling or buying past your 'fair' level.
Losses come from leaving your lane (macro, ETFs, bonds, crypto out of envy) and trading out of boredom in slow markets.
Avoid confirmation bias: read research that disagrees with your position.
Holding losers to protect ego usually ends worse by the close; exit intraday losers earlier.
Sunk cost of research time makes it harder to change your mind; heavy emotional attachment leads to oversized positions.
Do not get large ahead of a conference call.
notes: Event-driven/merger-arb trader. Main testable takeaway for MCF: news-driven moves should be traded with, not faded.

style: data scientist / educator (DataCamp), not a trader
edge_principles: Write automated tests on data (types, ranges, missing values, scaling errors such as extra zeros) before analysis; data cleaning is most of the work.
Prefer code over spreadsheets for reproducibility, diffable changes and separation of data from logic.
Small samples invite overfitting; always evaluate on out-of-sample/holdout data.
Start from the question, then decide what data answers it; interpretable models are easier to trust and act on than black boxes.
notes: Learning-to-code episode; no trading setups.

style: crypto OTC market maker (Cumberland/DRW)
edge_principles: Never assume; verify every operational step (addresses, settlements) in immature markets.
Volatile booms stress-test operations; manage cash and inventory efficiency and open settlement risk.
Easy cross-exchange arbitrage in major coins disappears as spreads tighten with new entrants.
notes: Crypto market structure update; no trading setups.

style: aggressive discretionary options trader moving to hybrid (scripted risk rules)
edge_principles: Stay alive until your market (high-volatility, momentum) returns; trade small or scratch in the rest.

Scripted behavioural 'seatbelts' built from own trade history: (a) per-symbol loss allowance shrinks with each consecutive loss in that name (e.g. 30-40% -> 20% -> 10%), then lock the symbol for 30-60 min after three straight losses; (b) positions larger than historical average size get tighter stops; (c) once a position is up 100%, lock the stop at break-even.
Separate instinct from stubbornness: once emotions attach and you justify a losing view, exit.
Long OTM options mostly expire worthless; only buy them when momentum is present and you are ready to cut fast.
Hold core swing ideas with more time so that sharp counter-moves do not shake you out; trade around the core.
Every algo bought from others eventually stopped working as markets changed; any edge needs ongoing upkeep.
Set aside money for taxes as gains accrue.
notes: Options trader's shift to short premium plus hedging, and a proposal for data-driven behavioural guardrails; the guardrail rules map directly onto MCF risk controls.

style: prop futures spread/inventory trader and trainer
markets: ASX bank bills, AU 3y/10y bond futures
edge_principles: Early edges (passive queue fills from clumsy VWAP/TWAP executions) decay as algos arrive and as size grows; plan to learn new skills before the plateau.
Deliberately spend a period practicing a weak skill (e.g. aggressive momentum entries) accepting lower P&L, with real money not simulation.
Trading is a skill set (reading flow, pattern recognition, execution speed, psychology), not just a strategy.
Think like a blackjack dealer: with a defined edge, single outcomes don't matter; judge trades by quality.
Reward good process, not P&L; a winning trade that broke the plan is a bad trade.
Don't turn a failing short-term trade into a long-term trade mid-trade; follow the pre-set plan, review it afterwards.
Avoid holding outright risk into major data releases or overnight; hedge when you cannot watch.
Hire traders for grit and demonstrated competitiveness; give new traders progression goals and a team.
Expect 6-12+ months to consistency; don't impose deadlines.
notes: Australian interest-rate futures spread trader; content mostly non-equity. Process principles relevant.

style: HFT options market maker / liquidity taker; crypto exchange founder
markets: Asian index options/futures, CME options, crypto
edge_principles: Edges that exploit a specific market mechanic (auction rules, lock periods) face less competition but are capped in size and vanish when exchange rules change.
Build infrastructure to try many strategies; run a portfolio of strategies so a few winners pay for many failures.
Backtest with a simulator that replays historical data and models latency and fill probability (queue, adverse moves).
Fees can be the whole edge for high-turnover strategies; high fees remove whole classes of strategies.
Spread small edges across many instruments to get enough independent bets per day.
Judge venue quality by top-of-book liquidity, not reported volume (crypto volume is often washed).
notes: HFT/exchange episode; not testable with MCF bar data.

style: prop intraday equities trader (small-cap fader, earlier sub-penny scalper and SSR specialist)
markets: US small caps, large-cap earnings gappers
edge_principles: Morning is the most mispriced period; most edge is gone by noon, so trade biggest early and be flat by midday.
Two red days in a row on a setup means change something: cut daily risk/lockout to 1/4 and go back to basics, then review stats.
Scale in with partial entries (start ~1/4) and scale out into washouts; you rarely pick the exact top.
Combine statistics (typical spike size and timing), fundamentals (filings, dilution), technicals and tape; size up as more align.
Record and quantify every occurrence of your setup (gap %, float, spike %, time of HOD/LOD, volume at checkpoints) to find repeatable ranges.
Edges built on market mechanics (algo prints, SSR fills) decay as more traders copy them and algos improve; keep researching new setups.
Pushing size for home runs hurt consistency; balance full size with taking profits.
notes: Highly practical small-cap fade process with quantifiable 'money box' and intraday volume-forecast tools; both testable on MCF 5-min bars.

style: prop futures spread trader (mean reversion), systematic rules executed manually
markets: AU and US bond futures, equity index futures, FX futures, crude, gold
edge_principles: Compare live results to tested expectations weekly; achieving ~80% of the tested payoff is the benchmark, and persistent shortfall (e.g. stops hit too often at a level) is monitored for a further month before changing rules.
Discretionary exits that are not in the test invalidate the test; don't exit early from fear during a drawdown.
Separate a normal drawdown (several strategies down 1-1.5 tested stops at once) from a broken strategy by checking each strategy against its tested drawdown.
Drawdowns often follow a size increase; scale up gradually because size tends to go up at the top of a wave.
Early mistakes: risking too much per trade and trailing stops too tightly, which cut winners on the first pullback.
Review same calendar month in prior years for seasonal changes in flows (e.g. quieter summer/daylight-saving periods).
Keep cash reserves so living costs never force decisions during a long drawdown.
Ideas come from observing the market; then collect data and test (Monte Carlo, forward test) before trading.
notes: Futures spread trader's drawdown and recovery; correlated-spread fade is portable to ETF pairs in MCF.

style: prop day trader; single-trade breakdown of the Lyft IPO
edge_principles: Have a thesis but only act when price action confirms it; be ready to trade either side.
Use reference levels (opening print, prior bounce highs, round numbers, volume-profile node) to judge who is in control.
Start with a partial size; add only as the trade works and stops can tighten.
Too much conviction sets up the biggest losses because you will not exit; size conviction trades with a defined stop.
Trade around a core position: cover a portion into big bids, re-short bounces; inability to re-short at a higher price is information.
Use resting (iceberg) orders at key levels so fast flushes fill you.
Plan risk in dollars per trade, then derive share size from the stop distance and liquidity.
notes: Detailed walk-through of trading Lyft's first day; IPO fade and round-number break rules can be partly tested if IPO first days are identifiable in MCF data.

style: prop equities trader (reversals, closing imbalances, event dislocations)
edge_principles: Never average down repeatedly: one bad doubled-down trade cost about a year's early profits; respect the stop and re-enter later if still valid.
If you find yourself hoping/begging a position turns, exit.
Losses are tolerable in high-volatility markets where opportunity is large; avoid big losses in dead markets where they take months to recover.
Keep a separate income or savings buffer so trading decisions are not driven by living costs.
Overnight/after-hours exposure (e.g. an unfilled closing order) can create sudden large losses; ensure every hedge/close order is confirmed.

Dislocations in thin derivatives (halted ETFs trading far below their underlying in a flash crash) are rare, high-probability opportunities; experience from earlier missed events builds the conviction to size up.
Watch overconfidence after winning streaks; return to small targets and only best setups after consecutive losing days.
Retention at prop firms is low (perhaps 15-30%); edges like U-code arb and imbalances decay over time.
notes: Prop trader's career lessons; panic-reversal setup is testable on MCF 5-min bars with a volatility regime filter.

style: investigative financial journalist (AFR), not a trader
edge_principles: Red flags for fragile companies: frequent capital raises, profits booked before cash is received, paying suppliers/staff with deeply discounted options, auditor switched to a tiny firm, founder selling and leaving the board, cash balance earning almost no interest (cash may be encumbered).
Being right on fundamentals is not enough for shorts: well-researched shorts doubled against holders before the collapse; manage position risk separately from the thesis.
Retail concentration in one speculative stock can wipe out savings; size so being 100% wrong does not ruin you.
notes: Corporate fraud investigations (Blue Sky, Big Un). No trading setups; fundamental red-flag checklist only.

style: retail full-time day trader (long-bias small caps); listener-question format
edge_principles: Sizing up in a non-risk-on market in an illiquid stock produced the trader's largest daily loss: earn size, but also check that conditions and liquidity justify it.
Start with one well-known pattern (flags/pennants, support and resistance) and master it before building a playbook.
Trade tiny real size first and set daily loss limits to avoid early blow-ups.
Keep 6+ months of living costs before going full time; side-trading (swing) while employed removes pressure.
Peer groups of active traders are often more useful than paid 'mentorship' to hundreds.
notes: Career-transition Q&A; no concrete setups.

style: crypto arbitrage/liquidity provision firm founder (2019 interview; firm later collapsed in the FTX fraud case)
edge_principles: Apparent arbitrages often vanish after counting fees, transfer limits, settlement time and counterparty/hack risk; model the full chain of costs.
Hedge for two reasons: positions with negative expected value, and positions whose size could threaten survival even if neutral EV.
Arbitrage profits come from serving imbalanced customer flow; exit on a different venue than you entered.
Treat automation as fast execution of human-chosen rules; humans set limits, required edge and sizing.
Chaotic markets offer the largest opportunities for those who can still price things correctly.
notes: Crypto market-making/arbitrage episode; not applicable to MCF data. Claims should be viewed in light of the firm's later collapse.

style: systematic long-only trend following / momentum on stocks
edge_principles: Keep the win rate around 40% or higher so the system stays psychologically executable.
Target profit factor and payoff ratio above ~2.
Study every drawdown, not only the maximum.
Use round, simple parameters and confirm a broad robust plateau (many lookbacks profitable), not a single peak.
Stress test by randomly perturbing closes by small percentages.
Avoid survivorship bias with historical index membership; generate signals on non-dividend-adjusted prices.
Diversify across several breakout lengths ('swarm') rather than picking one.
Use closing-price stops to avoid intraday spikes.
notes: Clear, fully specified daily/weekly system; also mentions a Bollinger Band breakout variant from his book. Good candidate for MCF daily-bar lab.

style: fixed income derivatives market maker turned crypto OTC/market-making firm founder
markets: interest rate futures/options, crypto spot and OTC
edge_principles: You should be able to state your edge in one or two sentences; otherwise it may be luck.
Edges from theoretical value decay quickly (often months); trade them in size while they last and keep innovating.
Avoid emotional attachment to trades; enter because of statistical expectancy.
Distrust unfalsifiable market commentary (e.g. vague 'test the level' calls); demand measurable predictions.
Price relative to related curves/instruments and ask why something is out of line before trading it.
notes: Career and crypto history (Cumberland, Silk Road coin auctions, OTC desk). Skeptical of chart-based TA. Prefers live small-size testing over long backtests. No MCF-testable stock setups.

style: systematic diversified trend follower (Mint Investments co-founder); now trades options long/short
markets: futures across many commodities and financials; options
edge_principles: The rule: cut losses and add to winners.
Spread bets across ~20 roughly uncorrelated markets, long and short; diversification lowers risk sharply and allows leverage.
Never enter without a stop; size each trade as (entry - stop) relative to core capital, a fixed fraction you can afford to lose.
Estimate odds by counting observable events (e.g. new highs/lows) in history; act only on positive expected value.
Be the house, not the punter: avoid bets that could put you out of the game.
Automate to stay disciplined; keep systems simple because simple is robust.
Early oversized trades nearly wiped him out; leverage plus concentration is the classic failure.
notes: Mostly life story and risk philosophy; no specific entry rules beyond generic new-high/low trend following. Typical trend-follower win rate cited ~35%.

style: exchange executive (former Nasdaq CEO); not a trader
edge_principles: Focus time on the few things that matter most and ignore the rest.
Incremental expansion from areas of strength compounds over time.
Exchange transaction revenue suffered under electronic competition; market data and index revenue were the steady cash flows.
notes: Corporate turnaround and market-structure history (Island/INET technology, ECN competition, listings competition). No trading setups.

style: intraday short seller of low-float micro caps; moved from retail to prop
edge_principles: Hard stops plus a daily loss lockout replaced 'mental stops', which caused rare but huge losses.
Never scale into a losing position; add only as price moves your way.
His stats showed he was usually too early; patience until the turn is where size can be used.
Place stops away from the obvious levels where all others on your side stop out.
Read the micro-cap regime (do runners continue or fade?) the way large-cap traders read the index.
Grow size incrementally (~10% steps) when doing well; cut back in drawdowns.
Prop advantages: zero commissions, rebates, many routes, peer review of trades.
notes: Mostly about moving to prop and running an office. One discretionary short setup; partly proxyable with MCF bars.

style: journalist/author on Jim Simons and Renaissance Technologies (not a trader)
edge_principles: Renaissance's edge came from earlier, cleaner, longer data histories and many small statistical signals combined in one shared model, not a single secret.
Signals are relational (stocks vs groups, index, factors), not calendar tricks.
Commodity/futures capacity is limited; equities stat arb was needed to scale.
Even top quants are tempted to override models in panics; stick with the model.
Avoid narrative-driven decisions; use data.
notes: Book interview (The Man Who Solved the Market). History, management culture, Markov models mention, tax controversy. No setups.

style: prop firm managing partner (7 Points Capital); occasional VIX/volatility trader
edge_principles: Daily lockout limits per trader; firm-level monitoring of concentrated exposure (e.g. crowded short squeeze/halt risk) and forced size reductions.
Cut size proactively as a monthly drawdown deepens; take days off when struggling; protect a good month from one bad day.
Increase size in small steps (10-20%), only when the trader can handle it.
Have a playbook of several strategies; a single crowded strategy (e.g. shorting low floats off the pre-market high) decays.
Traders get cut when they lose consistently or fail to adapt when last year's edge stops working.
Paper results do not count; real money emotions differ.
Accountability via trade review with an independent person; keep a life outside trading.
notes: Firm operations and trader management; no specific setups. Useful risk-governance ideas (daily loss limit, monthly drawdown size scaling).

style: founder of the WallStreetBets subreddit (community, not a trader)
edge_principles: Zero-commission apps and options/leveraged ETFs make extreme risk easy; most YOLO bets lose and some ruin lives.
Many who hit a big win admit it was not repeatable and quit; survivorship skews what gets posted.
Misunderstanding option assignment and margin can produce huge unintended exposure.
notes: Culture and anecdotes (Robinhood leverage glitch, assignment accident, fake trades). Cautionary; no setups.

style: former floor options market maker and bank equity-derivatives flow trader; crypto exchange co-founder (CoinFLEX, a show sponsor)
markets: index/bond options, OTC equity derivatives, crypto futures
edge_principles: Floor market making: small size for big-edge trades and recycle risk quickly.
Illiquid OTC risk is hard to exit; you may need to structure products to sell it off.
Always define take-profit and stop (bracket) at entry.
Physically delivered futures are harder to manipulate than cash-settled perpetuals referencing thin spot books.
notes: Career history and sponsor exchange promotion. No setups for MCF.

style: first-year full-time discretionary intraday scalper reading order flow
edge_principles: Keep only the capital you need in the trading account; leverage makes more unnecessary.
Sizing up too fast caused his largest drawdown (account from $20k to ~$8k).
Commissions as a % of profit decide which price ranges are viable for scalping.
Drop bias and trade what price/order flow shows; do not add to a loser hoping for a bounce.
Set review checkpoints (6-12 months) and a give-up point in advance.
Journal daily with annotated charts; playbook the best setups.
When opportunity is thin, step back rather than force trades; regimes change every few months.
notes: Newer trader profile; setups are discretionary order-flow scalps, only loosely testable.

guest: Compilation: Andy Kirschner, Blair Hull, Morad (FuturesTrader71), Doug Cifu, Sol Nasser, Dan Shapiro, Sam Bankman-Fried, Anthony Crudele
style: best-of compilation on risk management
markets: US equities, ES futures, options, crypto
edge_principles: Bet in proportion to edge but never more than ~1/50 of bankroll; after losing half the bankroll, halve bet size (Hull).
Regressive intraday sizing: cut size at 1/3, 1/2, 3/4 of the daily loss limit so the limit is hit with the smallest size and the most trades; add back size as P&L recovers (Morad).
Four consecutive losing days while following the plan means the regime changed: take a day off and review (Morad).
Traffic-light risk desk: warning at ~40% of daily stop, forced break and size cut at ~65-70%, hard stop at 100% (Sol).
Fixed 1% risk per trade; size from distance between entry and stop (Shapiro).
Review monthly that losing days stay of normal size; do not turn paper cuts into disasters.
Scale in with partial size (1/3) and add only when working; press only with profits above the day's risk budget (Crudele).
Holding big winners too long can turn large gains into large losses; have a structured exit plan (Kirschner).
Pre- and post-trade automated risk controls plus human oversight (Cifu).
notes: Compilation of earlier episodes; the one concrete setup comes from the ep66 clip. Strong set of risk-rule ideas that could become MCF portfolio guards (daily loss ladder, losing-streak pause).
